paragraphs: The paper studies how vision decides which side of an image boundary belongs to a nearer object and which belongs to the background. This assignment can change along a single contour, so the authors treat it as a collection of local decisions influenced by information from elsewhere in the image.

Their Bayesian belief network combines local evidence, including contour curvature and T-shaped junctions, with a broader description of shape. That description includes medial-axis structure: the skeletal organization of a region's interior. The proposed hypothesis is that this interior structure attracts ownership of surrounding borders, helping local boundary decisions form a coherent interpretation.

The authors also measure human judgments of border ownership at different distances from a T-junction. Human participants and the network produce similar spatial patterns along contours, with rapid convergence toward similar assignments. This agreement supports the proposed interaction between local cues and broader shape information as a computational account of figure–ground interpretation.
neurips-2010-a-bayesian-framework-for-fi.tldr: A Bayesian network combines local boundary cues with skeletal shape information to reproduce patterns of human figure–ground judgments.

paragraphs: A Diffusion Network models distributions over paths that vary continuously in both time and value. Its behavior follows stochastic differential equations, making digital simulation inconvenient. This paper develops an analog circuit implementation intended to let the network's continuous stochastic dynamics run in real time.

The design uses a logarithmic representation of the network's variables. The stated benefit is that the supply voltage, and therefore power consumption, can be reduced without restricting the dynamic range of the diffusion processes. This connects the choice of mathematical representation directly to a practical hardware objective: representing a broad range of behavior under a lower supply voltage.

The authors designed and fabricated a chip containing two stochastic units and describe its component circuits. They also present simulations of the complete system, which regenerate several kinds of continuous paths in real time. The reported simulation result supports the feasibility of the analog approach, while the fabricated two-unit chip establishes the concrete scale of the implementation described.
neurips-2010-a-log-domain-implementation.tldr: An analog, log-domain Diffusion Network design supports real-time path generation while allowing lower supply voltage without sacrificing dynamic range.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how temporary weakening of neuronal connections changes the behavior of a continuous attractor neural network. This weakening, called short-term synaptic depression, introduces a changing connection strength into the network's dynamics. The central question is how that change affects sustained activity and the processing of external inputs.

The authors find that the network can support both stationary and traveling concentrations of activity, described as bumps. They also find improved tracking of external inputs when synaptic depression is present. These results connect a short-term change in neuronal coupling with both stable activity patterns and the ability to follow changing stimulation.

A further finding is a slowly fading plateau after the network has been stimulated into an active state. Activity declines toward silence on the timescale of synaptic depression rather than the faster timescale of neural signaling. The authors argue that this behavior offers a possible mechanism for retaining short-term memories while allowing persistent activity to terminate naturally.
neurips-2010-attractor-dynamics-with-syn.tldr: Short-term synaptic depression improves input tracking and produces slowly fading activity that could support temporary memory in an attractor network.

paragraphs: The paper develops an algorithm for latent Dirichlet allocation that processes a text stream one document at a time. Its target setting is a stream large enough that retaining and repeatedly revisiting incoming documents is undesirable. Each document can be discarded after processing, so learning proceeds through the collection in a single pass.

The algorithm is deterministic and does not require keeping old statistics for every item in the data. These properties address two practical aspects of stream processing: making updates as documents arrive and avoiding a growing archive of per-document statistics. The contribution is therefore an approach to fitting the model under a different data-access pattern from batch learning.

In experiments, the proposed method runs much faster than a batch algorithm while achieving comparable perplexity. Perplexity supplies the stated basis for the quality comparison. The finding suggests that, in the evaluated settings, the computational advantages of processing each document once can be obtained while maintaining a similar level of model fit by that measure.
neurips-2010-deterministic-single-pass-a.tldr: A deterministic LDA algorithm processes documents once and discards them, achieving much faster learning with comparable experimental perplexity.

paragraphs: Energy disaggregation separates a home's total electricity signal into contributions from individual appliances. The motivation is that device-level information can help people conserve energy, whereas conventional meters provide only a household total. The paper tackles the computational problem of recovering useful appliance information from that combined measurement.

The authors extend sparse coding and train it specifically for disaggregation. Their method uses structured prediction to make the training discriminative: the learning objective targets performance on separating the appliance contributions. The important methodological choice is to shape the representation around the task the system ultimately needs to perform.

On a large-scale energy disaggregation task, the authors report a significant improvement over the sparse coding algorithms considered. They also illustrate how the resulting appliance estimates reveal useful information about energy usage. The demonstrated result concerns better disaggregation and informative outputs; the conservation motivation comes from the cited relationship between device-level information and user behavior.
neurips-2010-energy-disaggregation-via-d.tldr: Training sparse coding directly for appliance separation significantly improves its performance on a large-scale household energy disaggregation task.

paragraphs: Many statistical estimators minimize a loss plus a norm-based penalty. This paper examines how quickly gradient methods solve such problems when the number of variables can grow with, or exceed, the number of observations. In this setting, the global curvature assumptions used in classical optimization analysis may be unavailable.

The authors introduce restricted versions of strong convexity and smoothness and show that these hold with high probability for several statistical models. Under those conditions, Nesterov's first-order method converges geometrically until it reaches the model's statistical precision. That precision is measured by the typical distance between the estimated parameter and the unknown true parameter.

The guarantee ties useful computational accuracy to the accuracy supported by the data. Within that range, the geometric rate is substantially faster than the sublinear rates in previous analyses cited by the authors. The framework covers examples including Lasso, group sparsity, and nuclear-norm-based matrix recovery, making the connection relevant across several forms of high-dimensional estimation.
neurips-2010-fast-global-convergence-rat.tldr: Under restricted curvature conditions, a first-order method converges geometrically to the statistical precision of several high-dimensional estimators.

paragraphs: The paper studies variational Bayesian matrix factorization, a Bayesian approach explored as an alternative to classical singular value decomposition. Its optimization problem is nonconvex, which makes the distinction between a local optimum and the best solution across the entire objective especially important.

The main result is that the global optimum of the variational Bayesian matrix factorization problem can be computed analytically by solving a fourth-degree polynomial equation. This gives a direct route to the optimum despite the nonconvex formulation. The authors contrast it with a popular method based on iterated conditional modes, which reaches only a local optimum through repeated updates.

The result also extends to empirical variational Bayesian matrix factorization, where hyperparameters are learned from the data. Thus the analytic treatment covers both the factorization solution and a version that estimates additional model settings. Experiments illustrate the usefulness of these results. The central contribution is the global solution characterization, which removes reliance on a merely local solution for the formulations studied.
neurips-2010-global-analytic-solution-fo.tldr: The studied variational Bayesian matrix factorization problems admit analytic global solutions, including when hyperparameters are learned from data.

paragraphs: The paper considers prediction problems whose output is a graph describing dependencies among variables. The graph can change with the input: different values of a conditioning variable may imply different relationships among the variables being modeled. The authors call estimating this input-dependent dependency structure graph-valued regression.

Their method, Graph-optimized CART, divides the input space using a tree, following the broad structure of classification and regression trees. Each leaf contains an estimated graph. This gives the model a way to represent different dependency patterns in different input regions while retaining a tree-based organization of those regions.

The theoretical analysis uses dyadic partitioning trees and establishes oracle inequalities for risk minimization together with consistency of the tree partition. These results provide formal support for the method's estimation and partitioning behavior within that framework. An application to meteorological data illustrates how predicting a dependency graph can expose structure in complex data when one fixed graph would not express the intended conditional relationships.
neurips-2010-graph-valued-regression-ed1.tldr: Go-CART partitions the input space with a tree and estimates a dependency graph at each leaf.

paragraphs: Markov chain Monte Carlo uses a sequence of linked samples to estimate quantities of interest. This paper studies how changing the transitions of a finite Markov chain affects the long-run variance of such estimates. It begins with a reversible chain and constructs a nonreversible version with a theoretical performance guarantee.

The construction has a graphical interpretation: it inserts circulating flows, called vortices, into the state-transition graph. The method applies to reversible chains whose states are not connected through a tree. That structural condition matters because the stated transformation uses the connectivity available beyond a tree-shaped graph.

The authors prove that the transformed chain reduces the asymptotic variance of the associated MCMC estimator. The guarantee therefore concerns the variability of estimates in the long-run regime. Within the setting covered by the construction, it establishes a principled benefit from breaking reversibility and motivates further work on transition designs that exploit directed circulation to improve sampling performance.
neurips-2010-improving-the-asymptotic-pe.tldr: Adding directed circulation to suitable finite reversible Markov chains provably reduces the asymptotic variance of MCMC estimates.

paragraphs: The paper uses the television game Password to study how people reason about one another during communication. A speaker must convey a secret word using a one-word clue, and a hearer must infer the intended answer. This constrained exchange makes the interaction between clue selection and interpretation central to success.

Starting from the working hypothesis that human communication is relatively efficient, the authors test three predictions. Speakers and hearers should consider each other's perspectives, accurately anticipate each other's strategies, and share the cognitive work of communication roughly equally. These predictions distinguish taking another person's viewpoint from correctly understanding how that person actually approaches the task.

Game-show data provide evidence for all three predictions. The authors also find that efficient communication tends to deteriorate under time pressure. Together, the findings support a picture of communication as coordinated inference by both participants, with success depending on their ability to anticipate one another and distribute the reasoning effort during the exchange.
neurips-2010-inference-and-communication.tldr: Password game data support mutual perspective-taking, accurate strategy expectations, and shared cognitive effort, with efficiency deteriorating under time pressure.

paragraphs: Dynamic Bayesian networks often assume that the process governing a time series stays the same over time. This paper seeks more flexible models, addressing earlier approaches that either require discretized data or keep the network structure fixed. The objective is to accommodate changing relationships across time segments.

Greater flexibility also increases the risk of overfitting and uncertain inference, particularly when independent measurements are scarce. The authors investigate three different regularization schemes that share information across segments. The common idea is to support changing structure while allowing evidence from one segment to inform estimation in another.

The evaluation includes comparisons on simulated data and segmentation of gene-expression time series during fruit-fly embryogenesis. It also includes predicting a known five-gene regulatory network in yeast. These settings connect the methodological question to biological processes where relationships can vary over time and measurements may be limited. The stated contribution is the investigation and comparative evaluation of information-sharing schemes for this balance between flexibility and estimation stability.
neurips-2010-inter-time-segment-informat.tldr: The paper investigates three ways to share information across time segments when estimating dynamic Bayesian networks with changing structure.

paragraphs: The paper asks how useful internal representations emerge as information passes through a deep network. Deep architectures can express some learning problems efficiently and outperform local learning methods on some tasks, but that observation alone does not explain what successive layers contribute to the representation.

The authors develop an analysis based on Gaussian kernels to assess the learning problem at each layer. This provides a way to examine how the representation changes as the network constructs more abstract descriptions of its input. The focus is the progression through the network, allowing intermediate representations to be assessed alongside later ones.

Using this analysis, the authors find empirically that representations improve progressively through the layers. They also report that the best representations occur when discrimination is concentrated in the final layers. These findings connect the placement of discriminative processing with representation quality in the studied networks, offering evidence about how useful depth develops rather than only comparing final predictive outcomes.
neurips-2010-layer-wise-analysis-of-deep.tldr: A Gaussian-kernel analysis finds progressively better deep-network representations, with the best observed when discrimination occurs only in the final layers.

paragraphs: The paper addresses reinforcement learning methods that use L1 regularization to select features and reduce overfitting. Its main contribution is to express the regularized linear fixed-point problem as a linear complementarity problem. This reformulation changes how the problem can be solved and analyzed.

Compared with the LARS-TD formulation, the new approach permits efficient existing solvers, supports a new uniqueness result, and allows warm starts. A warm start reuses a starting point from a similar problem. That capability matters for policy iteration because successive evaluation and improvement steps create related problems whose solutions can inform later computation.

The authors demonstrate that warm starts and the efficiency of complementarity solvers can accelerate policy iteration. They also use warm starts to enable a form of modified policy iteration that approximates a greedy homotopy path. This generalizes the path considered by LARS-TD by bringing policy evaluation and policy optimization into the same construction, extending the role of the regularized solution path.
neurips-2010-linear-complementarity-for-.tldr: A linear complementarity formulation enables efficient solvers and warm starts for L1-regularized policy evaluation and improvement.

paragraphs: The paper develops an online variational Bayes algorithm for latent Dirichlet allocation, enabling topic modeling on very large document collections and incoming streams. The practical objective is to learn from documents as they are processed, making the approach suitable for collections whose scale makes batch fitting expensive.

The algorithm combines stochastic optimization with a natural-gradient update. The authors show convergence to a local optimum of the variational Bayes objective. This supplies a formal connection between the online updates and the objective being optimized, while preserving the qualification that the resulting optimum is local.

The evaluation includes fitting a model with 100 topics to 3.3 million Wikipedia articles in one pass. Across the reported comparisons, online LDA finds topic models as good as or better than those obtained with batch variational Bayes in a fraction of the time. The result demonstrates that the online learning strategy can deliver substantial computational savings alongside competitive topic-model quality at a large document scale.
neurips-2010-online-learning-for-latent-.tldr: Online variational Bayes scales LDA to millions of documents while matching or improving batch model quality in much less time.

paragraphs: The paper studies an agent acting in a finite stochastic environment while the reward function changes at every step. An oblivious adversary selects these rewards. The agent knows the transition probabilities but observes only its current state and the reward from its latest transition, leaving rewards for other choices unseen.

The objective is to compete in total reward with the best stationary policy. This creates a learning problem with both state-dependent transitions and limited feedback. The proposed algorithm addresses this setting under the assumption that stationary policies mix uniformly quickly, meaning their state distributions settle rapidly in a uniform way.

Under that assumption, the authors prove an expected regret bound of O(T^(2/3)(ln T)^(1/3)) after T steps. Because this grows more slowly than T, the average reward shortfall against the comparator decreases over time. The contribution strengthens the earlier no-regret result with an explicit convergence rate, described by the authors as the first rigorously established rate for this problem.
neurips-2010-online-markov-decision-proc.tldr: With known transitions and uniformly fast policy mixing, a new bandit-feedback MDP algorithm achieves an explicit sublinear expected regret bound.

paragraphs: The paper focuses on analyzing groups of related components within a network. In biological or social systems, a subnetwork may capture behavior that is difficult to understand from individual components alone. The authors propose a method that incorporates available network structure into the analysis of arbitrary subnetworks.

Their approach combines dimension reduction with statistical inference. It uses Laplacian eigenmaps with Neumann boundary conditions to obtain a reduced representation, then applies a group-penalized principal component regression model on graphs. The method brings information about network organization into both the representation of the data and the analysis of component groups.

The authors discuss asymptotic properties of the inference procedure in high-dimensional settings, together with choosing a tuning parameter to control the false positive rate. Simulated and real biological examples illustrate performance. The contribution is a framework for studying subnetworks as meaningful units while using dimension reduction to make their analysis more manageable and regularization to structure the resulting inference.
neurips-2010-penalized-principal-compone.tldr: The method combines graph-based dimension reduction and group-penalized regression to support statistical analysis of subnetworks.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a data-dependent way to measure the complexity of a hypothesis set. Its purpose is to connect the flexibility of candidate predictors with their behavior on unseen data. Because the quantity depends on the observed data, it supplies a sample-based ingredient for assessing generalization.

The proposed permutation complexity is related to Rademacher complexity and maximum discrepancy. Like maximum discrepancy, its construction uses dependent sampling. The authors prove a uniform generalization-error bound using this quantity. Uniformity means the guarantee applies across the hypothesis set, which makes the result relevant when a predictor is chosen from that set using the data.

A second result establishes concentration for the permutation estimate. The authors explain that this makes the complexity efficiently estimable. The two results address complementary needs: a complexity measure must support a useful generalization bound, and its value must be accessible enough to estimate. The paper supplies both a theoretical role and an estimation justification for the proposed measure.
neurips-2010-permutation-complexity-boun.tldr: A data-dependent permutation complexity yields a uniform generalization bound and a concentration result supporting efficient estimation.

paragraphs: Multi-task feature selection uses related learning problems to guide which inputs are retained. The paper examines joint sparsity penalties from the l1,q family, bringing commonly used l1,2 and l1,infinity penalties into one framework. Its central question is how to determine the appropriate member of that family for the task.

The authors give these penalties a probabilistic interpretation through the generalized normal distribution. They then construct a model using the noninformative Jeffreys prior. This connects the choice of sparsity penalty to model parameters that can be learned, making the shape of the regularization part of the estimation problem.

An extended version learns and uses more general pairwise relationships between tasks. For both versions, expectation-maximization algorithms estimate all model parameters, including q, automatically. Experiments cover two cancer-classification applications using microarray gene-expression data. The methodological contribution is a probabilistic route to adapting both feature-selection regularization and, in the extended model, the relationships through which tasks share information.
neurips-2010-probabilistic-multi-task-fe.tldr: A probabilistic model learns the sparsity penalty for multi-task feature selection and can also learn pairwise task relationships.

paragraphs: Semidefinite programs optimize over matrices constrained to be positive semidefinite. Random Conic Pursuit approaches these problems through repeated optimization over randomly selected two-dimensional subcones of the positive-semidefinite cone. Each step therefore works within a small part of the larger feasible geometry.

The authors present the scheme as simple to implement, scalable, and applicable to a broad range of semidefinite programs. Its stated tradeoff is solution precision: useful approximate solutions are readily available, but highly exact solutions are harder to obtain. This makes the approach particularly relevant when an approximate answer is sufficient for the application.

The paper argues that many machine-learning semidefinite programs fit that situation because they are based on random data, making exact minima less central. Experiments on several such problems demonstrate potential practical usefulness. A preliminary theoretical analysis also examines the algorithm's properties and convergence. Together, these contributions make a case for randomized low-dimensional optimization as a practical route to approximate semidefinite solutions.
neurips-2010-random-conic-pursuit-for-se.tldr: Random Conic Pursuit obtains useful approximate SDP solutions by repeatedly optimizing over random two-dimensional subcones.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to reduce the number of coordinates in a dataset while retaining an approximate guarantee for k-means clustering. Its result applies to any collection of n points in d dimensions. The reduced dimension is tied to the number of clusters and the desired approximation parameter.

The projection multiplies the data matrix by a random matrix whose entries are equally likely to be positive or negative 1/sqrt(t). For an approximation parameter epsilon between zero and one third, the stated target dimension is t = Omega(k/epsilon²). With constant probability, the projection preserves the optimal k-partition within a factor of 2 + epsilon.

This is an approximate, probabilistic preservation guarantee. The paper also provides an explicit computation-time bound for constructing the projected data, linking the theoretical guarantee to efficiency. A numerical implementation and experiments on a large face-image dataset support the reported speed and accuracy. The contribution shows how a simple random transformation can reduce dimensionality while retaining a quantified relationship to the original clustering problem.
neurips-2010-random-projections-for-k-me.tldr: A random sign projection reduces dimensions while preserving the optimal k-means partition within a 2 + epsilon factor with constant probability.

paragraphs: The paper examines how smoothness of a loss function affects the rate at which learning approaches the best risk available within a hypothesis class. Its excess-risk bound for empirical risk minimization depends on three ingredients: the loss's smoothness, the class's Rademacher complexity, and the best achievable risk, denoted L*.

The dependence on L* is central. For typical classes whose complexity scales as sqrt(R/n), the bound has terms of order RH/n and sqrt(L*RH/n). When L* is zero, the resulting rate is approximately RH/n, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Thus the guarantee becomes faster in the separable case, where the hypothesis class can achieve zero risk.

The authors also provide related guarantees for online and stochastic convex optimization of smooth, nonnegative objectives. Across these settings, the results show how smoothness can interact with a small achievable objective value to improve rates. The theoretical benefit is explicitly tied to those quantities and assumptions, connecting favorable problem structure with faster learning or optimization.
neurips-2010-smoothness-low-noise-and-fa.tldr: Smooth losses yield excess-risk bounds that improve when the best achievable risk is small, reaching an approximately 1/n rate in the separable case.

paragraphs: The paper revisits how Hodgkin–Huxley models represent the energy cost of neuronal action potentials. Sodium entry determines that efficiency, and the classic model admits about four times the minimum charge required for its depolarization. The motivating experimental observations indicate that mammalian neurons can operate much closer to the metabolic optimum.

The authors introduce a family of models intended to capture sodium entry and action-potential width while reproducing voltage-gated channel dynamics similar to those observed in mammalian neurons. This addresses a mismatch between the classic model's behavior and the more efficient action potentials described in the experimental evidence.

A single parameter varies the model across the reported range of observations, from cortical pyramidal neurons to Purkinje cells. The family therefore offers a compact way to represent differences among these central neurons while attending to both waveform properties and sodium use. The paper demonstrates the models' performance and discusses their properties, presenting the single-parameter construction as an economical framework for this range of neuronal behavior.
neurips-2010-sodium-entry-efficiency-dur.tldr: A single-parameter Hodgkin–Huxley model family captures observed sodium efficiency, spike width, and channel dynamics across several mammalian neuron types.

paragraphs: Camera-shake removal often assumes that the same blur acts everywhere in an image. The paper explains why this can be inadequate: camera rotation, motion outside the sensor plane, and differences in scene depth can produce blur that changes across the image. Its goal is to handle that spatial variation from a single blurred photograph.

The authors contribute a classification of camera-shake types and a method that combines two existing ideas. One is an overlap-add framework for spatially varying filtering; the other is a fast blind-deconvolution algorithm for spatially invariant filters. Their combination extends the restoration approach to blur whose form depends on image location.

The paper also introduces an evaluation setup that captures real camera shake while recording the corresponding spatially varying point-spread function. This links the observed degradation to a recorded description of its blur. Experiments demonstrate deblurring of images affected by spatially varying real camera shake, supporting the usefulness of accounting for variation across the image.
neurips-2010-space-variant-single-image-.tldr: A single-image deblurring method handles spatially varying camera shake and is evaluated using real blur with recorded point-spread functions.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn a probability distribution's support, the region where its probability mass resides, directly from data. The setting specifically allows the distribution to lack a density relative to a reference measure. This makes it important to estimate support without requiring a density-based description.

The authors propose regularized spectral estimators built around a new property of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, called complete regularity. Completely regular kernels capture relevant geometric and topological properties of a probability space. Their role is to give the estimation method access to the structure needed to distinguish the support.

These kernels are the key ingredient in the proof of universal consistency for the proposed estimators. The authors compare their role with that of universal kernels in supervised learning. Numerical experiments also show favorable comparisons with leading density-support estimation algorithms. The contribution therefore combines a consistency argument for the density-free setting with empirical evidence that the spectral approach can perform competitively.
neurips-2010-spectral-regularization-for.tldr: Completely regular kernels enable universally consistent spectral support estimation for distributions that need not have a density.

paragraphs: SpikeAnts explores how organized activity can emerge in a decentralized system. The paper focuses on division of labor in an ant colony, using a spiking-neuron network to model the decisions of individual ants and their interactions. The central question is how local communication produces collective patterns.

Each ant is represented by two competing spiking neurons. After receiving signals from neighboring ants, this competition determines whether the ant forages, sleeps, or grooms itself. The colony as a whole is a sparsely connected network, so collective behavior arises through the interactions among these small decision-making units.

The model produces three kinds of temporal behavior: asynchronous foraging, synchronized foraging, and synchronized periodic foraging. These patterns resemble behaviors found in some living colonies. The authors present a phase diagram showing how the patterns depend on two parameters representing sociability and receptivity. This relates changes in local interaction characteristics to changes in colony-wide organization and demonstrates synchronized activity within the proposed model.
neurips-2010-spikeants-a-spiking-neuron-.tldr: A sparse network with two spiking neurons per ant produces several colony-wide foraging patterns through local interactions.
